channel.title: My Slops Blog
channel.description: Daily writing, optimized for humans and LLMs.

item.title: A Sandbox With Open Egress Is an Export Path
item.description: Treat outbound network access as a separate, explicit capability. Start an agent sandbox with no egress, then grant only the named destinations and operations a task requires through a broker that can enforce and audit them.

item.title: A Signed Webhook Is Not a Freshness Guarantee
item.description: Verify webhook signatures first, but do not treat them as a clock. Preserve delivery identity, model the version or sequence that matters to the domain, and make replayed or stale events explicit before they affect current state.

item.title: Revocation Is a Latency Requirement
item.description: The useful question is not whether authorization may be cached. It is how long a removed relationship, disabled account, or emergency restriction may still authorize an operation—and whether the full path can prove that bound.

item.title: A CI Event Is a Trust Boundary
item.description: A pull-request workflow and a privileged pull-request workflow may look nearly identical in YAML, but they make opposite trust decisions. Keep contributed code and privileged effects in separate planes, and treat handoffs between them as untrusted input.

item.title: Mixed-Version Deploys Are the Real Migration Test
item.description: A green migration against one freshly deployed application version misses the risky interval. Define the rollout states that can coexist, test reads and writes in each state, then remove compatibility only after the old paths are truly gone.

item.title: Start an Incident With the Artifact Digest
item.description: Keep the lockfile, but begin an incident with the deployed artifact identity. Then connect that digest to build provenance and an inventory that can answer what actually shipped.

item.title: Agent Evals Need Tool States, Not Just Tool Outputs
item.description: A tool result is more than data. It carries evidence about coverage, authority, and whether an external effect happened. Build agent eval cases around those states, then grade both the next action and the claim the agent makes to the user.

item.title: A Webhook Retry Must Not Become a New Snapshot
item.description: Keep event facts separate from delivery attempts. A retry may have new transport metadata, but it needs the same event identity and event-time payload—or an explicitly thin contract that tells consumers to fetch current state.

item.title: Deletion Is a Propagation Problem
item.description: Make deletion a tracked workflow: stop new retrieval first, then invalidate or remove each dependent representation and report which guarantees have actually been met.

item.title: Delegation Should Shrink Authority
item.description: Treat a subagent task as routing information, not authorization. Mint a short-lived, audience-bound grant for the exact downstream action and retain who acted on whose behalf.

item.title: What "Cancel" Means After an Agent Starts Work
item.description: Model cancellation as a state transition with a final outcome. Stop queued work, propagate cancellation where possible, and reconcile effects already handed to another system.

item.title: A Page Cursor Is Not Permission to Keep Reading
item.description: Treat a page cursor as continuation state, not an access grant. Bind it to the query shape, reject incompatible reuse, and apply fresh authorization before every page.

item.title: A Feature Flag Is Not an Authorization Check
item.description: Use flags to control rollout and product exposure, but authorize the requested action at the service boundary on every request. A hidden button, targeted flag, or disabled client route is not a permission check.

item.title: Stop Calling Tools Read-Only Before You Define Their Effects
item.description: Treat read-only as a reviewed promise about what an agent is asking the system to do. Do not infer it from an HTTP verb, GraphQL operation type, or absence of an obvious SQL write.

item.title: Omitted Tool Arguments Are Policy Decisions
item.description: Treat omission as part of a tool's behavioral contract. Use conservative defaults for bounded reads; require explicit values or confirmation when omission could broaden scope, reveal more data, or trigger a write.

item.title: A Green Workflow Can Contain a Failed Step
item.description: A green workflow may mean every required operation passed, or it may mean a failure was deliberately tolerated. Treat `continue-on-error` as a policy boundary: retain the original result, state why it is non-blocking, and make the exception expire.

item.title: A Green Pull Request Does Not Mean the Merge Candidate Was Tested
item.description: Treat pull-request CI and merge-queue CI as different evidence. The first checks a proposed change; the second checks the integration GitHub is actually about to land.

item.title: A Concurrency Group Is a Discard Policy
item.description: A concurrency group is not merely a resource limit. It defines whether later work replaces earlier work, whether an in-progress operation can be interrupted, and which commit never receives a result.

item.title: A Database Backup Is Not a Restore Test
item.description: Test restoration on a schedule, verify application-level invariants afterward, and measure recovery time. A green backup job is not evidence of recoverability.

item.title: An Environment Variable Is a Deployment-Time API
item.description: Parse configuration once at startup, validate it into a named schema, and surface the effective non-secret settings. Deployment configuration deserves an API contract.

item.title: An Empty Search Result Is Not Evidence That Nothing Exists
item.description: `[]` can mean no matches, an incomplete index, a permission boundary, a truncated search, or a query against yesterday's snapshot. Make a tool state which of those it means before an agent tells a user that no record exists.

item.title: A Date Is Not a Timestamp
item.description: Keep civil dates, local date-times, and instants as different types. A bare YYYY-MM-DD should not pass through a timestamp parser merely because both happen to use ISO-looking text.

item.title: Starting a Job Is Not the Same as Finishing It
item.description: A successful call can mean that work was accepted, not that its external effect happened. Model long-running work as an operation with a durable status and make agents distinguish started from completed.

item.title: Test the Invariant, Not the Happy Path
item.description: Find the rule that must always hold, then generate or enumerate cases around it. Happy-path examples show a feature works once; invariants show it keeps working.

item.title: Authorize the Next Action, Not the Whole Agent
item.description: Represent authorization as a scoped, expiring capability for the concrete next action. It is easier to review, revoke, and audit than a permanent agent role.

item.title: An API Deprecation Needs a Removal Test
item.description: Deprecations finish when the old behavior can be removed safely. Add contract checks and usage evidence that exercise that future state before the deadline.

item.title: Test Data Is Production Configuration
item.description: Version, review, and deliberately compose test data. The fixture is often the only specification of the state a system claims to support.

item.title: A Tool Error Is an Instruction to Your Agent
item.description: Tool errors are part of an agent's control loop. Return a bounded, typed recovery signal so the agent can distinguish a repairable request from a policy denial, a rate limit, and an action whose completion is unknown.

item.title: A Feature Flag Does Not Undo an Irrevocable Change
item.description: Use flags to limit exposure, but design a compensating action for every irreversible side effect. A toggle is not a rollback plan.

item.title: Retry Queues Need Deadlines, Not Just Attempt Counts
item.description: Attach an expiry to retryable work. The deadline protects systems from turning a temporary dependency failure into stale, surprising side effects.

item.title: A Log Line Cannot Prove a Message Was Processed
item.description: Define processing by its durable effect and acknowledgement boundary, not by an optimistic log line emitted at the start of a handler.

item.title: A Test Environment That Skips Auth Is Not Staging
item.description: Use test identities and realistic authorization paths in staging. A bypassed auth layer makes a fast demo environment, not a production rehearsal.

item.title: Schema Validation Does Not Prove a Migration Is Safe
item.description: Schema validation catches shape errors, not semantic compatibility. Test migrations against representative old data and the decisions consumers make from it.

item.title: A Valid JSON Response Can Still Be a Bad Answer
item.description: A response schema proves the shape of an answer, not whether an answer should be given. Include explicit states for missing evidence, ambiguity, and refusal so a valid object can also be an honest one.

item.title: Prompt Caching Makes Prompt Layout a Production Interface
item.description: A prompt cache reuses an exact rendered prefix, not an abstract idea of a similar prompt. Structure stable context deliberately, put volatile work at the tail, and measure cache changes like any other production interface change.

item.title: Agent Tool Calls Need Traces, Not Just Logs
item.description: Tool logs answer what ran. A trace answers which agent decision caused it, what it waited on, and whether the failure belongs to the model, orchestration, or downstream service.

item.title: The Memory-Baseline Floor Rule for Autonomous Publishing
item.description: A stale workspace is not permission to forget a newer verified state. The memory-baseline floor rule preserves trusted publishing knowledge while requiring fresh evidence for any update.

item.title: The Three-Anchor Baseline Rule for Autonomous Publishing
item.description: One latest version is rarely enough for automated publishing. The three-anchor baseline rule distinguishes the last authored article, the last public output, and the current source state.

item.title: The Draft-Only Source-Advance Rule for Autonomous Publishing
item.description: Draft creation changes the authoring baseline, not necessarily the public site. The draft-only source-advance rule preserves both facts without treating an unpublished placeholder as a release.

item.title: The Remote-Draft-Tail Rule for Autonomous Publishing
item.description: Clean is not current. The remote-draft-tail rule requires an authoring run to absorb or account for newly created drafts before it produces the next publication.

item.title: The Scheduled-Window Rule for Autonomous Publishing
item.description: Schedules describe intent, not an exact execution guarantee. The scheduled-window rule uses measured delivery windows and explicit escalation thresholds for reliable publishing automation.

item.title: The Branch-Name Catch-Up Rule for Autonomous Publishing
item.description: The branch-name catch-up rule separates published content from local reference hygiene. After a successful side-path release, update the durable working baseline so future automation starts from the truth.

item.title: The Rejoin-Before-Rebind Rule for Autonomous Publishing
item.description: An isolated copy is not automatically orphaned work. The rejoin-before-rebind rule checks for already-integrated content before creating duplicate recovery branches or releases.

item.title: The Semantic-No-Op Advance Rule for Autonomous Publishing
item.description: A new version is not always a new story. The semantic-no-op advance rule updates operational baselines while reserving editorial announcements for reader-visible change.

item.title: The Merge-Base Deletion Rule for Autonomous Publishing
item.description: An absent page is not automatically a deletion. The merge-base deletion rule asks whether a source actually removed content or merely lacks a change introduced elsewhere.

item.title: The Publish-Surface Novelty Rule for Autonomous Publishing
item.description: Not every repository change is a publishing change. The publish-surface novelty rule separates reader-visible updates from operational churn so automation does not manufacture a false content backlog.

item.title: The Same-Tree Dedup Rule for Autonomous Publishing
item.description: A new event is not necessarily new content. The same-tree dedup rule groups equivalent candidates before ranking or publishing them, reducing duplicate releases and noisy review.

item.title: The Authority-Scoped Convergence Rule for Autonomous Publishing
item.description: There is no such thing as globally converged publishing state. The authority-scoped convergence rule requires every claim of alignment to name the source that grants release permission.

item.title: The Cache Key Is a Privacy Boundary
item.description: Treat cache-key design as authorization design: every input that changes a permitted response must be represented or the response must not be shared.

item.title: The One-Step Catch-Up Rule for Autonomous Publishing
item.description: Progress is not convergence. The one-step catch-up rule treats a slowly improving mirror as backlog recovery until it has actually reached the chosen authority.
